note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Apply the principles of customer service

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main aim of customer service in a hotel or villa?
options: To sell each guest as many extras as possible
To meet guests' needs so that they leave happy
To finish every guest request as fast as you can
To follow the rules even when they upset guests

questions.stem: Why is good customer service in tourism important to Jamaica as a whole?
options: It means hotels never need to train their staff
It lets the government stop collecting taxes
It means visitors do not need to pay for meals
Tourism earns foreign exchange and gives many jobs

questions.stem: Which of these is part of the service a restaurant guest receives, rather than the product?
options: The way the server greets and looks after them
The size of the portion that is put on the plate
The type of fish that is used in the main dish
The price of the dish as printed on the menu

questions.stem: A guest has stayed at the same villa in Ocho Rios every year for six years. Why is this good for the business?
options: Repeat guests never need any service at all
The villa can charge her double each time
It brings steady income at a low cost
Staff no longer need to clean her room

questions.stem: Who is responsible for good customer service at a hotel?
options: Only the manager and the staff at the front desk
Every member of staff, in every department
Only the staff who are given tips by the guests
Only the guest relations officer who is on duty

questions.stem: What usually happens when the service a guest receives is below what they expected?
options: They feel let down and may not come back
They are pleased because it cost them less
They forget about it as soon as they leave
They write to thank the staff for trying

questions.stem: Where do a guest's expectations of a hotel often come from?
options: Only the colour of the uniforms the staff wear
The weather forecast for the day that they arrive
The number of bedrooms that are on each floor
Its website, online reviews and what friends say

questions.stem: Which of these is an emotional need of a guest, rather than a physical need?
options: A cold drink on a hot day
A comfortable bed to sleep in
To feel welcome and valued
Clean towels in the bathroom

questions.stem: A family checks in at a villa after a long flight with two tired young children. What do they most likely need first?
options: A long talk about every tour on offer
A quick, easy check-in and a chance to rest
A full list of the villa's house rules to sign
A walk around the whole property with staff

questions.stem: A guest asks a front-desk agent for "somewhere nice to eat tonight". What is the best way to find out what she wants?
options: Ask what food she likes and what she will spend
Give her the name of the place your cousin owns
Tell her to look at the menus on the internet
Book the most costly restaurant in town for her

questions.stem: A business guest at a Kingston hotel asks for a wake-up call at 5:30 a.m. Why must the call be made on time?
options: The phone system only works early in the morning
Calls after 5:30 a.m. cost the hotel more
He may miss a flight or a meeting if it is late
It is the law that all calls are on time

questions.stem: Which is correct grooming for a server in a hotel restaurant?
options: Lots of rings, bracelets and chains, to look smart
Strong perfume or cologne, to cover kitchen smells
Own clothes for the day, if the uniform is in the wash
Clean uniform, hair tied back, short clean nails

questions.stem: Rohan is tired at the end of a long shift when a guest asks him for help. What should he do?
options: Tell the guest that his shift is nearly over
Help with the same care as at the start
Send the guest to find someone less busy
Help, but sigh so the guest knows he is tired

questions.stem: Why should staff not eat, chew gum or use their phones in front of guests?
options: It looks careless and makes guests feel ignored
It is only a problem if the manager is watching
Guests may ask to share the food or the gum too
Phones and gum are against the law in Jamaica

questions.stem: Why does a clean, tidy entrance and lobby matter to guests?
options: Guests only notice the bedrooms, not the lobby
It means the bedrooms do not need cleaning
It is part of the first impression of the property
It keeps the staff busy when there are no guests

questions.stem: A guest asks for a dish that is sold out. Which reply is the most positive?
options: "No, that's finished. Is there anything else?"
"You should have come earlier if you wanted that."
"That's not my problem. You would have to ask the chef."
"That's finished, but the jerk chicken is lovely."

questions.stem: How should staff usually address a guest whose name they know?
options: By title and surname, such as "Mrs Grant"
By a pet name such as "darling", to sound warm
By a nickname you have made up for the guest
By the room number, such as "Room 12", for speed

questions.stem: Why should you smile when you speak to a guest on the telephone?
options: The guest can see you on the phone screen
It makes the call cheaper for the hotel
A smile can be heard in your tone of voice
It stops the guest from asking questions

questions.stem: A caller has been on hold for a while, and the person they want is still busy. What should you do?
options: Leave them on hold until the person is free
Go back, explain and offer a call-back
Hang up, as they will call again if it matters
Put them through to any free extension

questions.stem: Which tone of voice is best when you explain a rule that a guest does not like?
options: Loud, so that the guest hears every word
Fast, so that the talk is over quickly
Bored, to show the rule is not yours
Calm, polite and firm, without arguing

questions.stem: A guest emails a villa to ask about airport transfers. What makes a good reply?
options: A prompt, polite answer with clear times and prices
A short reply a week later saying "call us"
A long reply full of text-message short forms
A reply in capital letters so it is easy to see

questions.stem: Two staff members are chatting loudly to each other about their weekend while guests wait at the bar. Why is this poor service?
options: The staff should only ever talk about work topics
The guests feel ignored and are kept waiting
The bar must be silent at all times
The guests might want to join the chat

questions.stem: Why should restaurant staff know what is in each dish on the menu?
options: So they can cook the dishes if the chef is late
So they can tell guests which dishes are cheapest
To answer questions on ingredients and allergies
Because guests are not allowed to ask the chef

questions.stem: A guest at a Negril hotel asks you to recommend a boat trip. What should you do?
options: Send them to a man on the beach who offers cheap rides
Tell them that boat trips are not safe in Jamaica
Say you do not know and walk away
Recommend a licensed operator that the hotel uses

questions.stem: Why should front-desk staff know the opening times of the spa, restaurant and gift shop?
options: So they can give guests correct information at once
So they can close them early when it is quiet
So they can work in each one when it opens
So they can tell guests to stay away from them

questions.stem: A guest asks for directions to a nearby attraction. Which is the best way to help?
options: Point in the general direction and wish them luck
Tell them to follow any car going that way
Give clear directions, a map and the travel time
Say it is too far and suggest they stay in

questions.stem: Which is a good example of suggestive selling by a server?
options: "You have to order a drink with that meal, sir."
"Would you like a glass of fresh sorrel with that?"
"Everybody here orders the most costly wine."
"Drinks cost extra, so you should just have water."

questions.stem: A guest who is blind comes into the hotel restaurant with a friend. How can the server help?
options: Take her arm and lead her to a table without asking
Speak loudly, because she will not hear well
Give the menu to her friend and talk only to him
Ask if she wants help, then read her the menu

questions.stem: A family with young children visits an attraction. Which action shows good service?
options: Show them the baby-changing room and play area
Tell them that children are best left at the hotel
Ask them to keep the children quiet the whole day
Charge each child the same price as an adult

questions.stem: A guest tells the server that he does not eat pork because of his religion. What should the server do?
options: Tell him a small amount of pork will not matter
Check with the chef which dishes have no pork
Suggest he picks the pork out of the dish
Ask him to explain his religion in detail

questions.stem: Which is an example of anticipating a guest's need?
options: Waiting until the guest asks three times for water
Clearing a table while the guests are still eating
Giving the bill before the guests have ordered
Bringing a high chair for a family with a baby

questions.stem: Kimone sees from the booking that a guest at the villa is celebrating her birthday. What could Kimone do?
options: Tell all the other guests the birthday guest's age
Ask the guest for a gift because it is her birthday
Arrange a card or small cake, if her supervisor agrees
Nothing, because a birthday is a private matter

questions.stem: Why should every guest get the same high standard of service, whether they tip or not?
options: Every guest deserves the same care and respect
So that guests who do not tip will feel ashamed
Because only guests who complain notice standards
So the supervisor cannot tell who gives tips

questions.stem: A guest's dinner order at a hotel restaurant was forgotten by the kitchen. What is the best way to put it right?
options: Blame the kitchen so the guest knows it was not you
Apologise, get the meal out fast and tell the supervisor
Say nothing and hope that the guest does not notice the wait
Tell the guest the kitchen is always slow on Fridays

questions.stem: A guest posts a poor online review about slow service at a restaurant. How should the manager reply?
options: Argue that the guest chose to come on the busiest night
Ask friends to post good reviews to hide it
Thank the guest, apologise and say what is being done
Ignore it, as online reviews do not matter

questions.stem: Why should staff pass on a guest's praise to the supervisor, as well as complaints?
options: So that the staff member can ask for a pay rise
Because praise must be paid for by the guest
So the supervisor knows who to blame next time
It shows what works well, so it is kept up

questions.stem: At the gate of an attraction, a vendor keeps pressing a visitor to buy, and she looks upset. What should you do?
options: Politely step in, guide her away and call security
Help the vendor by telling her the goods are cheap
Laugh it off, as this is a normal part of a visit
Tell her to buy something so that he will leave

questions.stem: The ticket line at an attraction is long and moving slowly. What is the best service?
options: Close the line so that no more guests can join it
Serve only the guests who complain the loudest
Tell guests how long the wait is likely to be
Take a break until the line gets shorter

questions.stem: A guest at an all-inclusive hotel offers you a tip, but the hotel does not allow staff to take tips. What should you do?
options: Take it quickly, before the supervisor can see you
Thank the guest and kindly explain the policy
Tell the guest that the tip is too small to accept
Take it, and share it with the supervisor later

questions.stem: A guest wants to pay a bar bill in US dollars. Which exchange rate should be used?
options: Any rate that the guest says is fair to him
The rate that the bartender heard on the news
The same rate that the hotel used last year
The rate the property has set for that day

questions.stem: A guest asks why the restaurant bill is more than the prices on the menu. What is the most likely reason?
options: GCT was added to the bill at the current rate
The server has added a tip for himself
Prices go up after 6 p.m. every evening
The till always adds a little extra by mistake

questions.stem: A guest asks if the beach at the villa is good for swimming today. There are strong currents. What should you say?
options: Say it is fine, so the guest is not disappointed
Say you are not allowed to talk about the sea
Warn about the currents and suggest a safer spot
Tell the guest to swim, but stay near the rocks

questions.stem: Why do the kitchen team and the restaurant team need to work closely together?
options: So that they can share the tips equally
The guest's meal depends on both doing their part
So that servers can cook when the kitchen is busy
Because they must take their breaks together

questions.stem: A well-known singer staying at a villa asks staff not to tell anyone that he is there. What should staff do?
options: Tell only a few close friends, not the public
Post a photo with him, since he is famous
Ask him why he wants it kept a secret
Respect his wish and keep his stay private

questions.stem: Villa guests are leaving for the airport. Which is the best way to say goodbye?
options: Wave from the kitchen window as their taxi leaves
Ask them to leave a big tip for the whole team
Thank them, wish them a safe trip and invite them back
Remind them to pay for anything they broke

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Team Jamaica is the training for people who work with visitors. Which organisation runs it? Give its short name.
What do we call each moment when a guest comes into contact with the business and forms an opinion of it?
What do we call the staff who deal with guests face to face, such as servers and front-desk agents?
What is the name for the stages a guest goes through, from booking, to arrival, through the stay, to leaving?
What do we call the cool drink, such as fruit punch, often given to guests as they arrive at a villa or resort?
What three letters are used for a guest who is very important to the business and is given special attention?
What word means making a place easy for everyone to reach and use, for example with ramps and wide doors for wheelchairs?
What is the job title of the hotel staff member whose main job is to help guests book tours, taxis and restaurants, and to give local information?
What do we call the person who shows visitors around an attraction and explains its history?
What do we call the record a hotel keeps of a guest's past stays and likes?
What do we call a guest who has a booking but does not arrive and does not cancel?
What do we call the time by which guests must leave their room on the last day of their stay?
On a bill in Jamaica, what do the letters GCT stand for?
What two-word term means putting things right for a guest after the service has gone wrong, so that they still leave happy?
What do we call it when happy guests tell family and friends about a business, so that more people come?

essays.stem: Describe the stages of the guest cycle at a villa, from booking to departure. Give one example of good service at each stage.
essays.modelAnswer: The guest cycle has four main stages. Before arrival, the guest books and asks questions. Good service is a prompt, polite reply with clear prices and details, and confirming the booking in writing. On arrival, the guest is welcomed. Good service is greeting them by name with a smile, offering a welcome drink, helping with the luggage and showing them round the villa. During the stay, staff meet the guest's needs. Good service is keeping the villa clean, dealing with requests quickly, and giving honest advice about local tours and beaches. At departure, the guest pays and leaves. Good service is having the bill ready and correct, helping with the luggage and the taxi, thanking them and inviting them back. After they leave, the villa may record the guest's likes and send a thank-you message, so the next stay is even better.
markingPoints: Names the stages: before arrival, arrival, the stay and departure (and after)
Good example before arrival: a prompt, clear reply and a written confirmation
Good example on arrival: welcome by name, welcome drink, help with luggage, show round
Good example during the stay: requests met quickly, clean villa, honest advice
Good example at departure: correct bill, thanks and invitation back; likes recorded

essays.stem: Explain how your grooming, posture and attitude affect the service a guest feels they receive. Give examples for a server or a front-desk agent.
essays.modelAnswer: Guests judge the service by what they see and feel, often in the first few seconds. A server in a clean, pressed uniform, with hair tied back, short clean nails and little jewellery, looks professional and hygienic, so guests trust the food. A front-desk agent who stands up straight, faces the guest, smiles and makes eye contact looks ready to help. Slouching, leaning on the counter, chewing gum or looking at a phone tells guests that they are not important. Attitude matters just as much. A positive, willing worker who greets guests warmly, stays calm when it is busy and offers help without being asked makes guests feel welcome and valued. A worker who sighs, argues or looks bored makes even a good meal or a lovely room feel poor. Good grooming, posture and attitude together build the guest's trust and make them want to come back.
markingPoints: Guests judge the service quickly by what they see
Grooming example: clean uniform, hair, nails, little jewellery; looks hygienic and professional
Posture example: standing straight, facing the guest, smiling; and what to avoid
A positive, willing, calm attitude makes guests feel valued
Links presentation and attitude to trust and to guests coming back

essays.stem: Explain the difference between a guest's physical needs and emotional needs. Give two examples of each from a hotel, villa or restaurant, and say how staff can meet them.
essays.modelAnswer: Physical needs are the things the body needs to be comfortable and safe. Emotional needs are about how the guest feels. Two physical needs are food and drink, and a clean, comfortable, cool room to sleep in. Staff meet these by serving good meals on time, offering water on a hot day, keeping rooms clean and making sure the air conditioning works. Two emotional needs are to feel welcome, and to feel safe and respected. Staff meet the need to feel welcome by greeting guests warmly, using their names and remembering what they like. They meet the need to feel safe and respected by keeping guests' details private, treating every guest fairly, and dealing with problems calmly and honestly. Good service meets both kinds of need: a perfect room is not enough if the guest feels ignored.
markingPoints: Physical needs: what the body needs for comfort and safety
Emotional needs: how the guest feels
Two correct examples of physical needs, and how staff meet them
Two correct examples of emotional needs, and how staff meet them
Says that good service meets both kinds of need

essays.stem: Explain how positive language and a good tone of voice help when you must say "no" to a guest. Give two examples of what you would say.
essays.modelAnswer: Guests do not like to hear "no", but the way we say it changes how they feel. Positive language tells the guest what we can do, not only what we cannot. A calm, warm and steady tone shows respect and keeps the guest calm, while a sharp or bored tone can turn a small problem into a complaint. First example: a guest asks for the fish, which is sold out. Instead of "No, it's finished," I say, "I'm sorry, the fish is finished tonight, but the jerk chicken is very popular. Would you like to try it?" Second example: a guest wants to check in at 10 a.m., but the room will not be ready until 3 p.m. I say, "Your room will be ready by 3 p.m. Until then you are welcome to relax by the pool, and we can keep your bags safe." The guest still gets a choice and feels looked after.
markingPoints: Positive language says what you can do, not only what you cannot
Tone: calm, warm and steady; a poor tone makes things worse
A first suitable example, with the words used
A second suitable example, with the words used
Offers a choice so that the guest feels looked after

essays.stem: Explain why staff need a good knowledge of the property's services and of the local area. Give examples of guest questions that they should be able to answer.
essays.modelAnswer: Guests expect staff to know their own property and the area around it. Good knowledge lets staff give correct answers at once, so guests save time, feel looked after and trust the property. It also helps the business, because guests use more of its services, such as the spa or the restaurant. Wrong or vague answers waste the guest's time and can even put them at risk, for example sending them to an unlicensed tour operator or to a beach with strong currents. Staff should be able to answer questions such as: What time is breakfast, and when does the pool close? Is there Wi-Fi? Which dishes have no nuts? How far is the nearest beach, pharmacy or bank? Which tours do you recommend, and are they licensed? How much is a taxi to the airport? If staff do not know an answer, they should find out and come back quickly.
markingPoints: Correct answers at once save the guest time and build trust
Helps the business, because guests use more of its services
Wrong answers waste time or can put guests at risk
Suitable examples of questions about the property's services
Suitable examples about the local area; finds out if unsure

essays.stem: Explain what is meant by anticipating a guest's needs and by exceeding a guest's expectations. Give examples from a villa or restaurant, and say what limits staff must keep to.
essays.modelAnswer: Anticipating a guest's needs means noticing what a guest will need and offering it before they ask. For example, a server brings a high chair when a family with a baby arrives, or a villa attendant puts out extra towels after seeing that the guests have come back from the beach. Exceeding expectations means giving a little more than the guest expected, so that they are pleasantly surprised. For example, villa staff see from the booking that it is a couple's anniversary and leave a card and some fresh fruit in the room, or a server remembers a returning guest's favourite drink. Staff must keep to limits. Anything that costs money or changes the rules needs the supervisor's approval. Staff must respect the guest's privacy and wishes, and must never promise what the property cannot deliver.
markingPoints: Anticipating: noticing a need and offering before the guest asks
A suitable example of anticipating a need
Exceeding expectations: giving more than the guest expected
A suitable example of exceeding expectations
Limits: approval for costs or rule changes, respect privacy, no false promises

essays.stem: A guest's airport pick-up did not arrive, so she took a taxi and reached the villa late, hot and upset. Describe how you would put things right.
essays.modelAnswer: This is service recovery: putting things right so the guest still leaves happy. I greet her at once, stay calm and listen to the whole story without interrupting. I apologise sincerely, without blaming the driver or anyone else, and say that I understand how tiring it must have been. I offer her a cold drink, help with her bags and get her room ready to use as soon as possible. Then I fix what I can. I tell my supervisor straight away and ask whether the villa will pay back the taxi fare or take it off the bill, since I cannot decide that myself. I tell the guest what will happen and when. Later I check that she has settled in and is happy. Last, I report the missed pick-up so that the cause is found and it does not happen to another guest.
markingPoints: Listens fully and stays calm
Apologises sincerely, without blaming anyone
Meets her needs at once: a drink, help with bags, the room ready
Asks the supervisor about any refund or cost; tells her what will happen
Follows up later, and reports the cause so it does not happen again

essays.stem: Describe how the different departments of a hotel (front office, housekeeping, kitchen, restaurant and maintenance) must work together to give a guest a smooth stay. Give examples.
essays.modelAnswer: A guest sees the hotel as one business, so every department must work together and pass on information. The front office takes the booking, notes special requests such as a baby cot or a food allergy, and passes them on. Housekeeping must have rooms clean and ready by check-in time, and tell the front office as each room is ready, so guests do not wait. The kitchen and the restaurant work together: servers pass on orders clearly and tell the chef about allergies, and the kitchen tells servers when a dish runs out. Maintenance repairs faults quickly, such as a broken air conditioner, after housekeeping or the front desk reports them. If one department lets the others down, the guest suffers. Good teamwork means clear messages, logs and handovers, helping each other at busy times, and respecting each other's work.
markingPoints: The guest sees one business; departments must share information
Front office passes on requests; housekeeping has rooms ready and reports when they are
Kitchen and restaurant: clear orders, allergies, dishes that run out
Maintenance fixes reported faults quickly
Good teamwork: clear messages and handovers, help at busy times

essays.stem: Explain how online reviews and social media posts by guests can affect a hotel or attraction, and describe how staff can help it earn good reviews.
essays.modelAnswer: Many travellers read online reviews and look at social media before they book. Good reviews and happy photos bring new guests at no cost to the business, while a few poor reviews can make people choose somewhere else. Reviews stay online for a long time and can be read all over the world. Staff help to earn good reviews by giving warm, steady service to every guest: greeting them by name, keeping rooms and public areas clean, serving food on time, giving honest advice and solving problems quickly, before the guest leaves. When something goes wrong, good service recovery often turns an unhappy guest into a loyal one. Staff should tell their supervisor about any problem they cannot fix, so that it is put right. Staff must never argue with guests online, or post guests' private details or photos.
markingPoints: Travellers read reviews before they book
Good reviews bring guests; poor reviews drive them away; reviews last and spread
Warm, steady service to every guest earns good reviews
Solves problems quickly, before the guest leaves, and reports what they cannot fix
Never argues online or posts guests' private details

essays.stem: Explain why visitors to Jamaica should be protected from harassment, and describe what staff at an attraction or on a resort beach can do to help visitors feel safe and welcome.
essays.modelAnswer: Harassment means pestering visitors, for example following them, pressing them to buy, or refusing to take no for an answer. It makes visitors feel unsafe and unhappy. They may stay inside their hotel, spend less money, write poor reviews and tell friends not to come, which harms tourism, the jobs it brings and Jamaica's good name. Staff can help by greeting visitors warmly, giving honest information, and recommending only licensed vendors, guides and taxis. If they see a visitor being pestered, they step in politely, guide the visitor away and call security or the supervisor, without arguing or fighting. They should know the rules of the property and the area, and report problems that keep happening. Staff who have done Team Jamaica training learn how to welcome visitors and show them the best of Jamaican hospitality.
markingPoints: Explains what harassment of visitors is
Harassment makes visitors feel unsafe and harms tourism, jobs and Jamaica's name
Warm welcome, honest information, licensed vendors, guides and taxis
Steps in politely and calls security or the supervisor, without fighting
Reports repeat problems; mentions Team Jamaica or similar training

practical1.title: Role play: welcome and look after guests through the guest cycle at a villa
practical1.brief: In the Centre's mock villa (or a mock front desk and lounge), the assessor gives the group four guest cards, for example: (1) a family with a baby, arriving tired after a long flight; (2) a couple celebrating an anniversary who want a dinner recommendation; (3) a guest who is blind and would like to know about the villa; (4) a guest who does not eat pork for religious reasons. Members take turns: for each card, one member is the villa staff member, one plays the guest, and the others observe and take notes on a checklist. Every member must play the staff member at least once and take the guest through the cycle: greet the guest by name, serve a non-alcoholic welcome drink, help with the luggage, explain the villa's services using the information sheet, find out the guest's needs with questions, meet one special request (for example, set up a high chair or baby cot, or check the menu with the "chef"), and later say goodbye. Each staff member then fills in a guest history card with the guest's likes. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, the guest history cards and the observers' notes to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Four guest cards from the assessor
The Centre's mock villa, or a mock front desk and lounge
A tray, clean glasses and a jug of fruit punch or water (non-alcoholic)
A villa information sheet and a sample menu
A high chair or baby cot, with the maker's instructions
photos: The greeting at the door, with open body language
The welcome drink being served from a tray
Explaining the villa's services with the information sheet
A special request being met, such as the high chair set up and checked
The menu being checked for a guest's dietary need
checklist: Greeted the guest promptly by name, with a smile and eye contact
Was well groomed, in a clean uniform, with good posture
Asked suitable questions to find out the guest's needs
Gave correct information about the villa's services in plain words
Met the special request correctly and safely, within their role
Used positive language and a warm, steady tone throughout
Said goodbye warmly, thanked the guest and invited them back
Filled in the guest history card clearly and correctly
safety: Serve non-alcoholic drinks only; wash your hands before handling glasses and drinks
Carry the tray with both hands or a flat hand underneath; wipe up spills at once
Set up the high chair or cot as the maker's instructions say, and check it is steady before use
Lift luggage safely: bend your knees and keep your back straight
Use only made-up guest names and details

practical2.title: Make a guest information sheet and answer guest questions at a mock tour desk
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a fact pack about a made-up resort in St Ann and its local area: opening times of the resort's facilities, the licensed tour operators and their tours, tour prices in J$ and US$ (set by the assessor), the nearest pharmacy, bank and beach, taxi fares, and the emergency numbers. As a group, make a one-page guest information sheet or poster in plain English that a visitor can read quickly. Every member writes at least one section. Then set up a mock tour desk. The assessor gives out guest question cards, for example: directions to the beach; a tour recommendation for a family; the price of a tour in US$; a request for a taxi to the airport; a guest who says a vendor keeps following her; a guest asking about swimming when the sea is rough. Members take turns as the desk agent, the guest and an observer. Every member answers at least one question face to face, using the sheet and the fact pack, and every member writes a reply to one email question from the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, the sheet and the email replies to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A fact pack from the assessor about a made-up resort and its local area
Guest question cards and email questions from the assessor
Flip chart or A3 paper, markers, rulers and a glue stick
A table and chairs for the mock tour desk
A computer or paper for the email replies
photos: The group reading the fact pack and planning the sheet
The finished information sheet or poster
The mock tour desk set up
A member answering a guest's question, using the sheet
The completed email replies (one from each member)
checklist: Wrote a section of the sheet that is correct, clear and easy to read
Greeted the guest and asked questions to find out what they needed
Gave correct, honest information from the fact pack
Recommended only licensed operators, and gave prices exactly as the fact pack set them
Dealt correctly with the vendor or sea-safety question, putting the guest's safety first
Used positive language and a friendly, steady tone
Wrote a prompt, polite and correct email reply, with no text-message short forms
Checked that the guest was satisfied, and thanked them
safety: Keep the desk area tidy, with bags and any cables out of the walkways
Give advice that keeps guests safe: licensed operators only, and honest warnings about the sea
Never say a guest's room number or details aloud
If you use a computer, sit with good posture and take short breaks
Use only made-up guest names and details
